title: A UK wholesaler's revenue was [[£8.25M]], not £8.91M: cancellations had been counted as sales
hub: A UK wholesaler's revenue was [[£8.25M]], not £8.91M: cancellations had been counted as sales
description: 541,909 invoice lines reconciled to 8.25M GBP of net revenue, RFM segments tested on the next quarter, and a ranking contest for retention targeting.
standfirst: A year of invoices ([[541,909]] lines) reconciles to [[£8.25M]] of net merchandise revenue from [[4,324]] customers. A first pass reported [[£8.91M]], [[8%]] too high, because cancelled purchases, postage and fees, duplicate rows and manual corrections had not been taken out. The bridge between the two figures closes to the penny.

p: Which customers deserve the retention budget? That needs a revenue figure you can trust first, then a segmentation, then a test of whether the segments predict anything.
The UCI Online Retail dataset: a UK online wholesaler's invoices from 1 December 2010 to 9 December 2011 (Chen, Sain and Guo 2012, CC BY 4.0). Many customers are themselves retailers.

Revenue is cleaned with a ledger that accounts for every pound: cancellations are netted against the purchase they reverse (matched on customer, product and unit price), postage, fees and adjustments are removed from merchandise revenue, and exact duplicate rows are dropped.

Customers are then scored by recency, frequency and monetary value (RFM) on data up to 9 September 2011 and checked against the next 13 weeks, which the scoring never saw. [[89.5%]] of Champions bought again, against [[58.4%]] of "At risk" customers. The labels carry signal, but "At risk" overstates the risk: in a wholesale business a quiet spell is often just the gap between orders.

For a retention campaign, four ways of ranking customers were compared. The top 20% by plain past spend held [[67.7%]] of next-quarter spend; a probabilistic value model (BG/NBD with Gamma-Gamma, written from its likelihoods) held [[69.3%]], a small gain for a much more complex method.

figure.alt: Waterfall chart from the first-pass revenue of 8.91 million pounds down to net revenue of 8.25 million, removing duplicates, postage and fees, cancelled purchases and manual corrections.
figure.caption: From the first pass (£8.91M) to net merchandise revenue (£8.25M): duplicate rows -£24K, postage, fees and adjustments -£150K, cancelled purchases -£448K, manual corrections -£39K. Data: results/metrics.json.

limits: One year of data, so no seasonality can be learned; the analysis is of revenue, not margin.
[[135,080]] lines without a customer ID (£1.45M) sit outside the customer view.
The December 2010 cohort includes established customers, so the cohort charts start optimistic.
The customer-value model is a likelihood fit to one wholesaler; it says nothing about other kinds of retailer.

p: The first version of this analysis reported [[£8.91M]] of revenue from [[4,338]] customers. It dropped cancelled invoices but not the purchases they cancelled. Those figures are retired. In the corrected data, Champions hold [[53.6%]] of net revenue.
